extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and history of science (readers of Bacon/Aristotle studies)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the methodological strengths and defects in Aristotle's physical researches (why many of his physical conclusions failed), as discussed in a historical/intellectual context. Focuses on empirical practice, forms of induction, conceptual clarity, and the role of authority and final causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect of facts / disregard of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: His neglect of facts (or, as it has been otherwise phrased, his disregard of experience)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a thinker collects and attends to relevant empirical facts. The page notes that the charge is inaccurately stated—Aristotle collected many facts (e.g. History of Animals) but they may be 'not always be well selected or precisely described.' Critiques point to reliance on others' authority and occasional inaccuracy or insufficiency in observations (see references to Whewell, Lewes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partiality for abstract reasoning
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether abstract reasoning is used appropriately; the text concedes abstract reasoning is essential if 'properly conducted' and should be balanced with empirical accumulation. Do not penalize abstraction per se—penalize when it supplants or ignores needed empirical verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of distinctness and appropriateness of ideas to facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A want of distinctness and of appropriateness to the facts in the Ideas he employs
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the concepts and ideas deployed are precise and well-suited to the observed facts. The page treats this as a well-grounded charge (cited from Whewell) and asks 'Why are Aristotle's ideas inappropriate to his facts?' — look for mismatch between conceptual apparatus and empirical material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of verification
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify whether different modes of proof confirm each other (e.g., induction confirmed by deduction or vice versa). The text defines verification as 'the confirmation of one mode of proof by another' and criticises Aristotle for often failing to confirm a priori arguments by inductive examination of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inaccurate or insufficient observations
rubrics_metrics.description: His observations, though very numerous and often very carefully conducted, were not infrequently inaccurate or insufficient, owing either to his own defects as an observer or ... to his relying too implicitly on the authority of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the accuracy, sufficiency, and independence of observational data. Examples and citations (Lewes, Quarterly Review) are given where Aristotle's observations are shown erroneous or inadequately described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rare use of experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Though it cannot be said with truth that Aristotle never tried experiments, still it must be confessed that he did so very rarely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the extent to which experimental testing is employed. The page gives rare examples Aristotle did use (removal of testes, eyes from young birds, removing hearts from tortoises) and notes that experiments are largely absent outside physiology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of traditional beliefs without investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: He frequently adopted traditional beliefs or stories ... without any further investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for unexamined reliance on prevailing lore or authoritative stories (examples: lion has one bone in neck, hen-partridge impregnated by hearing). Such acceptance of tradition without testing is a methodological defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hasty generalisation / Simple Enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of induction which he usually employs is that of Simple Enumeration ... he naturally lapsed into the habit of generalising on insufficient data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate simple enumeration from scientific induction: selection of instances (as Bacon insists) vs mere enumeration. Penalize generalisations based on scanty sampling and lack of methodological selection of cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vague use of general terms (lack of conceptual precision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's vague use of general terms. Words like motion, hot and cold, moist and dry, heavy and light, generation and corruption, natural and unnatural, &c., are employed simply in their popular acceptation, without any attempt to give them a definite and precise meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether key terms are precisely defined. Vagueness in core terminology leads to imprecise problems and unscientific results; evaluate clarity and operationalization of concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias from metaphysical preconceptions / seeking illustrations of preconceived maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: He was often diverted ... by his eagerness to discover illustrations of his favourite metaphysical distinctions ... His partiality for assigning the final rather than the efficient causes of phenomena is specially to be noticed ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the investigator seeks data to illustrate preconceptions (e.g., four causes, categories) rather than letting facts dictate theory. Such a priori modes of investigation can pervert facts or lead to erroneous generalisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to select instances (importance of selecting rather than merely enumerating)
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection of instances as distinct from their enumeration (the point on which Bacon so constantly and emphatically insists) would, doubtless, have done much to transform the philosophy of the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate methodological attention to selecting informative, discriminating cases (negative and positive instances) rather than mere accumulation. The text contrasts modern induction with ancient enumeration and recommends deliberate selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on authority and uncritical repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: The fault was in the scholars, who, instead of carrying on the master's work, contented themselves with blindly bowing to his authority, and repeating his maxims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether subsequent investigators critically engage with sources or merely defer to canonical authority. Blind deference impedes progress and provokes reactionary responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity and poor translations impeding understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: The inaccuracy and obscurity of the translations ... it would have been better if they had never been made ... 'malas translationes' ... Latinis ... receiving bad translations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate clarity and fidelity of textual transmission: poor translations or obscure language can generate misunderstanding, discourage inquiry, and lead to propagation of errors (Roger Bacon's complaint about translations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between empiricism and theoretic/explanatory aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract reasoning, provided it be properly conducted, is quite as essential a factor of science, as is the accumulation of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work balances collection of facts and sound theoretical reasoning; both are necessary. Penalize extremes (pure theory without verification or blind empiricism without conceptual framework).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of function/adaptation in biological inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of function, which implies so much of the idea of Final Cause ... is a conception absolutely essential to the successful prosecution of at least one science, that of physiology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In biological/physiological contexts, evaluate attention to function/adaptation. The page argues that final-cause-style reasoning (adaptation/function) can be legitimate and necessary in physiology and should not be categorically excluded from natural theology or broader views of design.
